description: Test your knowledge of PA RS1 | Respiratory System. Focus on pneumonia classification, pathogenesis, and clinical correlations for MBBS students.

cards.text: What is the pathological definition of pneumonia?
cards.answer: Infection-driven inflammation of the lung parenchyma (alveoli and/or terminal airways).

tip.tip: ALVEOLI are the functional gas-exchange units where infection spreads

cards.text: What is the principal causative agent of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) in immunocompetent adults, and what radiographic pattern does it characteristically produce?
cards.answer: Streptococcus pneumoniae, causing a classical lobar consolidation pattern.

tip.tip: S. pneumo = typical CAP → LOBAR pattern (entire lobe involved)

cards.text: When does hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) occur, and what is the typical microbial flora?
cards.answer: Onset >48 hours after admission; typically Gram-negative rods (Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, Enterobacter) and MRSA.

tip.tip: HAP >48hrs = flora shifts to GRAM-NEGATIVE rods + MRSA (nosocomial pathogens)

cards.text: Why does aspiration pneumonia typically involve the right lower lobe?
cards.answer: The right main bronchus is wider and more vertical, allowing preferential passage of aspirated material by gravity.

tip.tip: GRAVITY + wider RIGHT bronchus = right-sided aspiration (right middle lobe if semi-upright)

cards.text: Name the most common cause of atypical pneumonia in young adults and list a key microbiological difference from typical organisms.
cards.answer: Mycoplasma pneumoniae; atypical organisms lack peptidoglycan cell walls or are intracellular, making them Gram-stain negative and unresponsive to beta-lactams.

tip.tip: ATYPICAL = no peptidoglycan = Gram-NEGATIVE + beta-lactam RESISTANT

cards.text: List the four major lung defence mechanisms that, when impaired, predispose to pneumonia.
cards.answer: Mucociliary clearance, alveolar macrophage function, resistance to overwhelming inoculum, and immune response to organism virulence factors.

cards.text: What are the four sequential stages of lobar pneumonia and their approximate timeline?
cards.answer: Stage 1 - Congestion (Days 1-2, serous exudate); Stage 2 - Red Hepatisation (Days 3-4, fibrin and RBCs); Stage 3 - Grey Hepatisation (Days 5-7, neutrophil infiltrate); Stage 4 - Resolution (Days 8+, macrophage clearance).

cards.text: What is the characteristic sputum appearance in Klebsiella pneumoniae pneumonia, and in what patient population is it classically observed?
cards.answer: "Currant jelly" sputum (blood-stained, thick, purulent) in alcoholic patients or those with underlying chronic lung disease.

tip.tip: ALCOHOL + KLEBSIELLA = CURRANT JELLY sputum (distinctive bloody, viscous finding)
